Organising & Hospital Administration

Organising the work, hospital administration, departments, organisational structure and the nurse’s place in it.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Describe the process of organising
  • Describe the structure of a hospital
  • Explain the nursing department structure
  • Relate organisational charts to duties

In simple words

Organising is arranging tasks, people and equipment so that the plan can be carried out. Every hospital has an organisational chart showing who reports to whom.

Steps in organising

  1. Identify and group the activities to be done
  2. Assign activities to people and departments
  3. Define authority and responsibility
  4. Establish relationships and communication channels
  5. Obtain and arrange equipment and supplies

Hospital departments

Department Work
Medical Consultation and nursing care
Surgical Operation theatres and post-operative care
Laboratory and imaging Diagnostics
Pharmacy Medicines and stores
Nursing Inpatient and outpatient care
Support Dietary, laundry, housekeeping, records
Administration HR, finance, legal

Nursing department hierarchy

Nursing superintendent → deputy nursing superintendent → ward in-charge / charge nurse → staff nurse → nursing assistant

🔴 Empowerment, not overload

Duty that is allocated must be supported with knowledge, information and equipment. Unclear authority causes overload, error and complaints.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Organising = grouping tasks, assigning people and defining authority.
  2. Hospital departments: medical, surgical, nursing, laboratory, pharmacy, support.
  3. Nursing hierarchy: nursing superintendent to staff nurse.
  4. Written duties clarify roles and reporting.
  5. Nursing department manages inpatient, outpatient and community care.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Organisational charts show the reporting lines.
  2. Committees coordinate quality, infection control and pharmacy.
  3. Clinical nurse specialists add expertise to the nursing team.
  4. Procedures and standing orders reduce uncertainty.
  5. Emergency plans must name authority and roles.

📌 Memory trick

Organising: Group, Assign, Authority, Communication, Equipment (G-A-A-C-E).

60-second revision

  • Organising: group activities, assign people, define authority.
  • Hospital departments and their roles.
  • Nursing hierarchy from superintendent to staff nurse.
  • Clear reporting avoids duplication and error.
  • Written duties and org charts support care.

Test yourself

Organising mainly outputs:

Answer: B. Organising produces structure with defined roles, duties and reporting relationships.

The first step in organising is to:

Answer: B. Organising begins with identifying and grouping the activities to be performed.

Who heads the nursing department in a hospital?

Answer: A. The nursing superintendent or matron heads nursing services.

A clear reporting channel in a ward ensures:

Answer: B. Clear reporting lines avoid duplication and delay, and make escalation of problems quick.

Committees in a hospital are mainly for:

Answer: A. Committees such as infection control and quality committees coordinate care and monitor standards.
